messages.content:
RoadDraft is a headless 2D CAD engine for roadway plans. Model space is US survey feet, and a point is [x, y] = [easting, northing] -- the other way round from how coordinates are usually spoken, so N 5000, E 2000 is [2000, 5000]. Sheets are paper inches seen through viewports at a feet-per-inch scale. Work through the commands: each one validates its params and explains what was wrong, every change is journaled and undoable. Start with get_document_state to see what is in the document, list_commands for the full surface, and render_sheet or render_model to look at your work.

To annotate something, find it before you point at it. In a sheet file the design usually lives in a referenced basefile, so the document owns no geometry of its own; find_entities searches the attachments too. Filter by what a thing IS -- layer, type, or its design anchor -- rather than dumping the document: find_entities {anchor: {kind: 'offset', offset: [-12, 12]}, visible_on: 'C-102'} is the pavement edges that sheet shows. Then pass the id straight to place_callout as target_entity, and the engine puts the leader tip on the geometry. Do not compute the point yourself: the midpoint of a curve's endpoints is not on the curve, and roadway linework runs parallel a few feet apart, so a hand-computed point usually lands on the wrong line rather than on nothing. If you do pass a raw target point, read the warning that comes back -- it names what the tip actually touched.

Some things are not entities at all -- a station, a PC, a point at an offset. Ask the design for those: list_alignments with include_references=true names a referenced alignment 'DESIGN:SR-100', and station_to_xy, xy_to_station, resolve_anchor and get_design_data all accept that name and answer in host coordinates. To call one out, give place_callout a target_anchor ('18+00@12R', 'PC-1'; BC-1 and EC-1 name the PC and PT too) and that alignment name. Otherwise commands do not take it: nothing can be drawn, labelled or anchored to an alignment this document does not own.

Plan annotation belongs on the sheet, in paper inches, not in the model. Pass the sheet as place_callout's space and still name a model target -- target_entity or target_anchor: the engine sees it through the sheet's viewport (scale and twist included) and puts the tip where it shows on the paper. 'at' then runs along the part of the entity that sheet shows, since a pavement edge runs the whole project and a sheet shows one stretch. find_entities with visible_on gives each row a sheet_point, which is where that tip will land -- use it to choose a position for the text that is clear of the linework. Never work out a viewport by hand: model_to_sheet and sheet_to_model convert, and station_to_xy and point_on_entity take a sheet and answer in paper inches as well.

Drafting from a description works the same way: give the engine the description, not coordinates you worked out. A bearing and distance goes in as written -- create_alignment takes start + legs (each leg a bearing, azimuth or deflection and the distance to the next PI, with the radius of the curve at the PI it starts from), draw_traverse draws lines and curves course by course, and traverse computes the points without drawing. offset_entity copies linework parallel at a distance (one entity, or a chain offset as one path), fillet rounds the corner between two lines with a curve (a curb return), and measure with along gives distances along a line, chain or alignment and square off it. key_points and snap give the exact endpoints, intersections, centers and alignment design points (PI, BC, EC) to build on. Station-and-offset drafting is draw_station_offset with the stations and offsets given ('30+00@12R'). Linework drawn through something is cut back with trim (a point on the part to cut away) or run on with extend, not redrawn from computed points; break, join, lengthen, chamfer, copy, rotate, mirror, scale and array edit what is there. create_points sets COGO points, label_segments letters bearings and distances or L1/C1 tags with line and curve tables, place_along sets blocks or points at an interval, hatch fills an area (a point inside is enough), and area and get_entity read areas, lengths, bearings and curve data off the drawing.

Do one drafting task in a headless CAD engine called RoadDraft, using the tools you have been given. They are your ENTIRE tool surface.

Rules:
- Every change to the drawing must go through a tool call.
- The document is already open and saves itself after each command. Do not save it under another name.
- Nobody can answer questions. Work until you judge the task done, then stop and give your report.
- You have no calculator and no code execution. Any arithmetic you need, do yourself.

THE TASK:
Create alignment SR-9, beginning at station 50+00, through these points (easting, northing): begin at (1000, 1000); a PI at (2200, 1000) with an 800 ft radius curve; end at (3100, 1900). Draw its centerline on layer align_MAIN.

When finished, reply briefly with:
1. What you created and drew (names, layers, key coordinates).
2. The tool calls that mattered, in order (tool name + the key arguments).
3. Anything that failed, confused you, or that you had to work around -- quote error messages. If you had to compute coordinates yourself, show the arithmetic.

messages.reasoning:
Let me understand the task:
1. Create an alignment called "SR-9"
2. Beginning station: 50+00 (which is 5000 feet)
3. Points:
   - Begin at (1000, 1000) - easting, northing
   - A PI at (2200, 1000) with an 800 ft radius curve
   - End at (3100, 1900)
4. Draw its centerline on layer "align_MAIN"

Looking at the create_alignment tool, I need to provide:
- name: "SR-9"
- begin_station: "50+00" or 5000
- pis: array of [x, y] or [x, y, radius] points
- start: [easting, northing] = [1000, 1000]

Wait, let me re-read the description for create_alignment:
"The roadway stationing engine. Entity-chain mode (path_ids + begin_station): walk connected line/polyline/arc entities. Design mode (alignment=NAME): use the alignment's true stations and equations and anchor every tick and label. Either way it draws perpendicular ticks at the interval, '12+34.56' labels rotated along the path, and BC/EC/PCC/PRC labels at the curve points."

And create_alignment says:
"Create a horizontal alignment in the design model from PIs ([x, y] at BEGIN/END, [x, y, R] interior), from bearings and distances (start + legs: each leg a bearing, azimuth or deflection and the distance to the next PI, with the radius of the curve at the PI it starts from), or from CoordGeom elements; optional begin station (display, '10+00') and station equations. x is the easting and y the northing, so N 5000, E 2000 is [2000, 5000]. Given legs, the engine computes the PIs -- no trigonometry by hand -- and get_design_data kind=tangents reads the bearings and lengths back. 

Alignments are pure design data: draw_alignment puts linework in model space, annotate_stationing/place_label label it."

So create_alignment accepts either:
1. pis: [x, y] or [x, y, radius] points
2. legs: bearings/distances
3. elements: tangent/curve objects

The problem specifies a PI at (2200, 1000) with an 800 ft radius curve. I'm using the pis format with radius included. The begin point is (1000, 1000), the PI is at (2200, 1000) with R=800, and the end is (3100, 1900). Since there's a curve specified at the intermediate point, this indicates a curved segment connecting the first two points.

For a simple tangent curve layout, the alignment would be a straight line from the beginning through the PI to the end, then a curve around the PI radius. But that doesn't match how curves work in CAD—typically the curve radius applies between tangents, not at a single point. Reconsidering: if the curve starts at the PI, then the first segment (beginning to PI) should be tangent, and the curve begins there heading toward the end point. So the structure is straight from (1000, 1000) to (2200, 1000), then a curve with 800 ft radius starting at the PI, continuing to the final point.

In LandXML-style notation, the pis parameter takes coordinates with radius values at points where curves begin. For this case, I'd have: begin at [1000, 1000], the PI at [2200, 1000, 800] indicating the curve starts there, and end at [3100, 1900]. This assumes a tangent segment before the PI since there's no radius specified for the first coordinate.

But looking more carefully at the schema, all interior points accept [x, y, R] format. Since only the middle point has a radius value, the first and last points are just tangent transitions. The actual challenge here is figuring out the curve geometry itself—I can't assume it's a simple circular arc without calculating where the tangents meet and what direction the curve needs to bend.

If I treat the PI as the center of an 800-foot radius circle, the starting point (1000, 1000) sits 1200 feet west of it, placing the beginning at approximately -70 degrees from eastward. To reach (3100, 1900) from that center, I'd need to find where the 800-foot radius intersects that direction—but the direct distance check shows this approach might not yield a valid connection.

Rather than forcing a circular arc centered at the PI, I should reconsider whether the radius specification actually defines a circular curve between the PI and endpoint instead.

A simpler path uses the PI as a turning point: drive straight from the start to the PI at (2200, 1000), then apply an 800 ft radius left turn to connect to the final destination. Using a three-element layout—tangent from origin to PI, curve at PI with 800 ft radius, tangent continuation—should produce the intended geometry. In LandXML terms, this means marking the PI coordinate with the radius value to signal the curve begins there.

However, examining the coordinate geometry more closely reveals something important: moving from (1000, 1000) to (2200, 1000) runs directly east, but reaching (3100, 1900) from (2200, 1000) requires a sharp right-angle turn followed by additional eastward travel. An 800 ft radius curve may not naturally achieve this exact connection without careful angular calculations. Let me verify this by calculating the angle needed. From PC to PT would be atan2(900, 900) = 45°, so the delta would be roughly 135° - 45° = 90°. With R=800, that gives T ≈ 585.8 ft and L ≈ 754.4 ft, putting the PT at station 5850.8, which doesn't match the expected (3100, 1900) location.

I realize I'm making this too complicated. The most straightforward path is a simple traverse: move from (1000, 1000) to (2200, 1000) directly east for 1200 ft, then continue from there.

Actually, looking at the coordinates again—the problem likely wants me to define an alignment with a specific curve geometry rather than a complex multi-segment route. I should test whether a basic definition using the provided points works correctly before adding unnecessary complexity.

If I use [1000, 1000] as the start and [2200, 1000, 800] as the second point, the system might interpret this as an 800-foot radius curve starting at (2200, 1000) and extending toward the end point at (3100, 1900). The challenge is determining what happens when the first point has no radius specification—the system could treat it as a tangent approaching the curve, or it might require both points to explicitly define a circular arc section. I'll experiment with creating the alignment using the pis array format and see how the system handles the undefined radius at the first point.

Good - the document is open, has no geometry yet, and layer "align_MAIN" exists. Now I need to create alignment SR-9 with the specified points:
- Begin at (1000, 1000) at station 50+00
- PI at (2200, 1000) with 800 ft radius curve
- End at (3100, 1900)

I'll use create_alignment with pis parameter. The format for pis is [x, y] or [x, y, radius] for interior PIs.
